clue.text: American on the river is an existentialist

indicators.note: in a down-the-page sense, placed on means coming after the earlier piece

parts.note: the Cam is the river that flows through Cambridge
US is short for American, as in the United States

explanation.surface: An American found by a riverbank turns out to be a philosopher of the absurd.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Camus, the French author of The Outsider, is widely classed among the existentialist writers.

clue.text: Macedonian king, prepared to murder, and caress, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests a possible rearrangement of the letters of the words and caress

explanation.surface: A ruthless Macedonian monarch alternates between killing and tender caresses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges AND CARESS. Cassander had Alexander the Great's mother, widow and son killed to secure the throne.
explanation.definitionFit: Cassander ruled Macedon after Alexander's death and had Alexander's heirs put to death.

clue.text: Reportedly most significant poems of Richard Eberhart

indicators.note: reportedly signals that we want a word that is spoken like the one meaning most significant

parts.note: main means chief or most significant

explanation.surface: Rumour has it these are the most important poems of the American poet Richard Eberhart.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Eberhart, an American poet, published a collection called Maine Poems; the US state's name is said like 'main'.
explanation.definitionFit: The New England state gives its name to Eberhart's collection Maine Poems.

clue.text: If Twain's out of order, it's satirical

indicators.note: out of order means the letters of If Twain's are jumbled into a new sequence

parts.note: here Twain's stands for Twain is, so its S counts as a letter

explanation.surface: If Mark Twain is misbehaving, his writing is bound to be satirical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of order' rearranges IFTWAINS. The 's of Twain's is a contraction of 'is', so its S stays in.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonathan Swift, author of Gulliver's Travels, is the model satirist, so his adjective means biting and satirical.

clue.text: Architect sells piece of open countryside?

parts.note: to hawk goods is to sell them, usually door to door
a moor is a stretch of open, uncultivated upland

explanation.surface: A designer of buildings disposes of a patch of open land, perhaps to a developer.
explanation.walkthrough: Nicholas Hawksmoor was an English Baroque architect who worked with Wren.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas Hawksmoor designed several London churches and parts of Oxford colleges in the English Baroque style.

clue.text: W . H. Davies produced one of magic

definitions.text: W . H. Davies produced one of magic

parts.words: W . H. Davies produced one of magic
parts.note: the Welsh poet W. H. Davies wrote a poem and collection titled with a span of time 'of Magic'; the clue asks for that unit of time

explanation.surface: The tramp-poet W. H. Davies conjured up something magical.
explanation.definitionFit: Davies's 1922 collection was called The Hour of Magic, so the 'one' is a sixty-minute period.

clue.text: French composer possibly Black Forest devil?

explanation.surface: A French composer may have been a demon from the German woodland.
explanation.walkthrough: In German Wald is forest and Teufel is devil; the Black Forest is the Schwarzwald, which is why the second sense carries 'possibly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Émile Waldteufel was the Alsace-born composer of The Skaters' Waltz, and his surname is German for a forest demon.

clue.text: Sounding like child-worker

parts.note: a son is someone's male child
a worker ant is the standard crossword worker

explanation.surface: Someone sounds just like a young labourer.
explanation.definitionFit: In phonetics a sonant is a voiced sound, so as an adjective it means sounding or voiced.

clue.text: Parts which must be included in revision of a glib obit

indicators.note: a revision reworks the text, so the letters of a glib obit are rearranged

explanation.surface: An editor's rewrite of a slick obituary insists on keeping certain sections.
explanation.definitionFit: In music obbligato parts are the essential accompanying lines that must not be left out; this is the Italian plural.

clue.text: Asimov character is really switched on

definitions.text: Asimov character is really switched on

parts.words: Asimov character is really switched on
parts.note: an Asimov figure is a machine, so being switched on describes it literally rather than meaning alert

explanation.surface: A figure in an Isaac Asimov story is wonderfully bright and alert.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac Asimov wrote I, Robot, and his mechanical men literally come to life when powered up.

clue.text: Incorporeal, like Graves's Quixote?

explanation.surface: Something without a body resembles a knight-errant from a book by Graves.
explanation.walkthrough: This is Richard Graves, an 18th-century novelist, not Robert Graves: his novel was The Spiritual Quixote.
explanation.definitionFit: Incorporeal means relating to the soul rather than the body; Richard Graves's novel was The Spiritual Quixote, about a Methodist zealot.

clue.text: "A savage old—, with an immense fortune" (Macaulay, Lord Clive )

definitions.text: "A savage old—, with an immense fortune" (Macaulay, Lord Clive )

parts.words: "A savage old—, with an immense fortune" (Macaulay, Lord Clive )
parts.note: the missing word in Macaulay's essay on Clive is a term for a man who came home rich from India

explanation.surface: A quotation from Macaulay's essay on Lord Clive with one word left blank.
explanation.definitionFit: The word, from Urdu nawab, was applied to Britons who returned from India with enormous wealth, as Macaulay does here.

clue.text: Spies associated with the sick by Powell?

definitions.text: associated with the sick by Powell

explanation.surface: Anthony Powell links a ring of spies with people who are unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Powell's 1936 novel is Agents and Patients, pairing this word with the sick.
explanation.definitionFit: Secret operatives are spies; Powell's title couples them with patients, that is, the sick.

clue.text: Russian sectarian is German, by the way

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
by in the sense of plus or along with is und, German for and
ist is the German for is

explanation.surface: A member of a Russian religious sect turns out, incidentally, to be German.
explanation.walkthrough: 'German' turns both 'is' and 'by' into German words; 'by the way' reads as a throwaway phrase but splits up.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stundists were a 19th-century Russian Protestant sect, named after the German Stunde, an hour of Bible study.

clue.text: Thomas's were in the skin trade

definitions.text: Thomas's were in the skin trade

parts.words: Thomas's were in the skin trade
parts.note: Dylan Thomas left an unfinished novel whose title says that certain exploits happened in the skin trade

explanation.surface: Someone called Thomas worked in the leather or fur business.
explanation.definitionFit: Dylan Thomas's unfinished novel is Adventures in the Skin Trade, so his escapades were in the skin trade.

clue.text: Crawford's imperial physician?

parts.note: F. Marion Crawford wrote a novel whose title joins a medical title to the name of a Roman emperor

explanation.surface: A novelist called Crawford has a doctor who serves an emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: F. Marion Crawford's 1883 novel is Dr Claudius; its title is a doctor bearing an imperial Roman name.

clue.text: Fowles protagonist school of Nabokov?

explanation.surface: A character in John Fowles belongs to the same school as Nabokov.
explanation.walkthrough: Fowles's novel The Collector has a butterfly-hunting kidnapper; Nabokov was a passionate lepidopterist, so his 'school' is that of butterfly hunters.
explanation.definitionFit: Frederick Clegg, the butterfly enthusiast of Fowles's first novel, gives its title; Nabokov too gathered and studied butterflies.

clue.text: Aldous Huxley's visual impairment culminates here?

definitions.text: Aldous Huxley's visual impairment culminates here?

parts.words: Aldous Huxley's visual impairment culminates here?
parts.note: Huxley, himself nearly blind, wrote a novel whose title places a sightless state in a particular city

explanation.surface: The near-blind Aldous Huxley's eyesight problems come to a head at a particular place.
explanation.definitionFit: Huxley's novel Eyeless in Gaza takes its title from Milton's Samson Agonistes, where the blinded Samson is held.

clue.text: Wharton is possibly historical novelist

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of Wharton is might be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: Edith Wharton might count as a writer of historical fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges WHARTONIS. William Harrison Ainsworth wrote Old St Paul's and The Tower of London.
explanation.definitionFit: William Harrison Ainsworth wrote many Victorian novels set in the past, such as Rookwood and Old St Paul's.

clue.text: Representative of Miller's work

explanation.surface: A figure stands for the plays of Arthur Miller.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Miller's play is Death of a Salesman.
explanation.definitionFit: A sales representative sells goods for a firm, and Miller's play Death of a Salesman features one, Willy Loman.

clue.text: Name assumed by Thomas Browne, planning armed robbery

definitions.text: Name assumed by Thomas Browne, planning armed robbery

parts.words: Name assumed by Thomas Browne, planning armed robbery
parts.note: Thomas Alexander Browne, the Australian novelist of Robbery Under Arms, wrote under a pen name; the first part of it is wanted

explanation.surface: A man called Thomas Browne takes an alias while plotting a hold-up at gunpoint.
explanation.walkthrough: Not Sir Thomas Browne of Religio Medici: this is the Australian Thomas Alexander Browne, who signed himself Rolf Boldrewood.
explanation.definitionFit: The pseudonym Rolf Boldrewood was used by Thomas Alexander Browne for Robbery Under Arms, the bushranger novel.

clue.text: Characters from violent era may bring about apocalypse

indicators.note: bringing about means turning round, so the letters of violent era are reordered

explanation.surface: A violent age could herald the end of the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may bring about' rearranges VIOLENTERA, the characters of 'violent era'.
explanation.definitionFit: Apocalypse is Greek for an unveiling, and the last book of the Bible goes by both names.

clue.text: "Behold, David is in the wilderness of — " (Book of Samuel)

definitions.text: "Behold, David is in the wilderness of — " (Book of Samuel)

parts.words: "Behold, David is in the wilderness of — " (Book of Samuel)
parts.note: the gap in the verse from 1 Samuel 24 is the name of an oasis by the Dead Sea where David hid from Saul

explanation.surface: A verse from the Book of Samuel with the place name left out.
explanation.definitionFit: In 1 Samuel 24 Saul is told that David hides in the desert of the oasis En-gedi, beside the Dead Sea.

clue.text: Vaughan saw it the other night

definitions.text: Vaughan saw it the other night

parts.words: Vaughan saw it the other night
parts.note: Henry Vaughan's poem The World opens by claiming he saw something endless on a recent evening

explanation.surface: The poet Vaughan spotted something just the other evening.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Vaughan's The World begins 'I saw Eternity the other night, Like a great ring of pure and endless light'.

clue.text: Furnish with English joke

parts.note: a quip is a witty remark or joke

explanation.surface: Supply someone with an English wisecrack.
explanation.definitionFit: To furnish a person or place is to provide it with what it needs, to fit it out.

clue.text: Trainee in the lower deck becomes Nobel Prizewinner

indicators.note: in tells us the learner is placed inside the word for lower deck

parts.note: below means on a lower deck of a ship
L, from learner plates, stands for a trainee

explanation.surface: A naval recruit on the lower deck goes on to win a Nobel Prize.
explanation.walkthrough: Saul Bellow won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1976.
explanation.definitionFit: Saul Bellow, author of Herzog and Humboldt's Gift, received the 1976 Nobel Prize in Literature.

clue.text: A mere poet, perhaps

parts.note: mere here is a lake, so a poet of the lakes, like Wordsworth, is meant rather than a minor poet

explanation.surface: Someone who is only a poet, nothing more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mere' looks like 'only' but is the noun for a lake, as in Windermere.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lake Poets, Wordsworth, Coleridge and Southey, lived in England's Lake District, so each was called by this name.

clue.text: Holmes elucidated one of four

parts.note: Sherlock Holmes solved a case in a Conan Doyle novel titled with a mark 'of Four'

explanation.surface: Sherlock Holmes explained one of a group of four.
explanation.definitionFit: Conan Doyle's second Holmes novel is The Sign of Four, the mark left by four conspirators.

clue.text: 'We shall be at Hebron before they — their eyelids' (Disraeli, Tancred)

definitions.text: 'We shall be at Hebron before they — their eyelids' (Disraeli, Tancred)

parts.words: 'We shall be at Hebron before they — their eyelids' (Disraeli, Tancred)
parts.note: the missing verb in Disraeli's line means to loosen or undo, here used of waking eyes

explanation.surface: A line from Disraeli's novel Tancred with one verb left blank.
explanation.definitionFit: To loosen a knot is to undo it; Disraeli pictures sleepers unfastening their eyelids as they wake.

clue.text: Grisham's reincarnation of 23's Henderson?

parts.note: Bellow's novel is Henderson the Rain King, and John Grisham wrote a legal thriller with a similar title

explanation.surface: John Grisham's book revives the hero of a Saul Bellow novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 23 is BELLOW: Saul Bellow wrote Henderson the Rain King, so Grisham's The Rainmaker seems a later version of him.
explanation.definitionFit: Grisham's novel The Rainmaker echoes Henderson, Bellow's hero who becomes a rain king in Africa.

clue.text: Author a law unto himself

parts.note: a historian coined a famous law about bureaucracy and named it after himself, so the idiom is meant literally

explanation.surface: A writer who acts as a law unto himself, ignoring all rules.
explanation.definitionFit: C. Northcote Parkinson formulated Parkinson's Law: work expands to fill the time available.

clue.text: Elizabeth Bowen wrote to it

parts.note: Bowen's 1932 novel has a title addressed 'To the' plus a compass point, so she seems to write to a direction

explanation.surface: The novelist Elizabeth Bowen sent a letter somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth Bowen's novel is To the North, its title naming a compass point.
